properties.description:
`export_surface` now keeps any Verification whose `VERIFIES` edge lands on a published Interface or a published Requirement, and `SurfaceExport.evidence` names them — carried through to both MCP reply shapes, because a disclosure the caller cannot see is not a disclosure that was reported.

⭐ WHY. Delivery is computed as SATISFIED and REALIZED and A PASSING CHECK. A consumer receiving a published promise and no check could not tell whether it currently HOLDS — so the surface handed across a claim nothing can re-run. That is exactly the defect this design removed from its own insides on 2026-09-22 (241 capabilities reading "verified", 21 with a check anything could re-run), reproduced at the seam.

🛑 DERIVED, NOT A THIRD OPT-IN, and the reason is measured. Interfaces and Requirements each travel on an explicit `designation`; a third gate on Verification would reproduce the failure measured the same day — 262 requirements, ZERO marked `published`, because the vocabulary existed and nothing asked. THE OWNER ALREADY OPTED IN WHEN THEY PUBLISHED THE TARGET.

SCOPED TO THE COMMITMENTS, not to everything on the surface. A Component travels because a published contract needs its sides, not because anyone undertook anything about it, so a check on that component stays home. Measured on this design: 3 of 315 Verifications travel.

⚠️ AND IT DISCLOSES, WHICH IS WHY `evidence` NAMES RATHER THAN COUNTS. A check travels AS STORED — trimming one would make it import as a lie — and `findings` is free text. Measured on the three that travel here: internal build paths (`target/debug/...`), internal ChangeEvent ids and internal node counts, all in that field. Bounded, real, and now readable by the owner before the surface leaves rather than discoverable in somebody else's graph.
properties.name: A published surface carries the checks for what it published, and names which ones left
